transcript:
Header:
Date/Time: 2026-09-14 16:30 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Olivia Park (Head of ML, Iridium), Samir Patel (Infra Lead), Ellen Wu (VP Eng)

Summary: quick cost / unit economics discovery. Customer evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private for inference. Focus on per-token pricing, batching/caching levers, budget constraints, and SLOs for latency. They want a pilot and rough TCO for Q4.

Topics: per-token tiers, batching KV cache, reserved capacity economics, latency vs cost tradeoffs, security/compliance requirements (SOC2, KMS), next steps for pilot and benchmarks.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone thanks for joining, uh we appreciate the time. Quick intros then we'll jump into what you're trying to achieve on cost.
[00:12] Olivia Park: hi, Olivia here, head of ML. We're evaluating inference for a suite of assistants and downstream risk models. Main ask is keep latency under 200ms P95 for our core workflows and hold overall monthly cloud spend to a cap.
[00:25] Maya Chen: great. Diego, quick background on what we'll cover?
[00:28] Diego Ramos: yeah hi all. I'll run through how Redwood approaches cost per token, batching, KV cache, and how dedicated/reserved can change unit economics. We'll go through some example math with your expected qps and seq lengths.
[00:40] [00:40] Samir Patel: quick note — infra constraints: we use EKS in us-east, some workloads must stay in VPC, and a subset of models will need on-prem eventually.
[00:48] Diego Ramos: noted, that maps to our hosted vs private options and dedicated.

[01:02] Olivia Park: to be concrete, our average generation call is around 350 tokens with 12ms client-side pre and post processing, peak qps ~120 for the assistant flows, embeddings at lower rate. We saw token counts spike during long threads, though.
[01:18] Maya Chen: ok so two levers — per-token price and batching/caching to reduce effective tokens served. For hosted we have per-token pricing tiers (we'll send the sheet) and inc. a small network fee; dedicated is commit-based so unit cost drops with reserve.
[01:33] Samir Patel: can you walk through an example? like hosted per-token cost vs dedicated with reserved GPUs?
[01:38] Diego Ramos: sure. Rough example — hosted per-token might be X cents per 1K tokens at base model, but with your volumes dedicated reserved capacity amortizes GPU cost so effective per-token can be 30-60% lower depending on utilization. The big caveat is utilization — if you underutilize reserved GPUs costs can be higher.
[01:58] Ellen Wu: how does batching factor in? we worry about P95 latency, not just average.
[02:03] Diego Ramos: batching increases throughput but can add latency. Our runtime does dynamic batching and latency-aware routing — requests that need strict P95 can bypass batching or use small batch sizes. Also prefix/KV cache preserves tokens by avoiding recomputation for repeated prefixes, so your effective token billing drops.
[02:22] [02:22] Olivia Park: KV cache — does it reduce billing or just latency?
[02:25] Diego Ramos: both. By caching the KV for prefixes you avoid re-sending and re-computing the same tokens. Billing-wise, your downstream model still produces tokens for the continuation, but you avoid repeated context processing. In practice for assistants with stable prompts we've seen 15-40% token reduction.
[02:40] Samir Patel: what's the operational complexity to enable KV cache on Dedicated vs Hosted?
[02:45] Diego Ramos: on Hosted it's largely transparent — we manage caches per-tenant. On Dedicated you get full control; you can tune cache sizes, TTLs, and even pin to GPUs. For Private on-prem we'll ship the same runtime but you'd manage the cache lifecycle.
[02:58] Maya Chen: also look at quantization and model choice — smaller quantized variants reduce cost per token but may affect response quality; Redwood Optimize helps recommend quantization profiles per workload.
[03:12] [03:12] Olivia Park: okay, we care about hallucination and QA, so quality regressions are a risk. How do you measure quality regression when changing model or quantization?
[03:20] Diego Ramos: we tie eval sets to rollouts. Our Console can run prompt-based evals and alert on quality regression; you can pin model versions during canary. We'll share a short guide.
[03:30] Ellen Wu: back to economics — can you give a sample TCO for our 120 qps peak and average call size?
[03:37] Diego Ramos: quick back-of-envelope. If avg tokens per call 350 and 120 qps sustained peak, that's ~42k tokens/sec peak, about 3.6B tokens per day at peak sustained — this is just an example. With hosted per-token $0.XX per 1k tokens you can map to monthly. With Dedicated, if you reserve N A100-equivalent GPUs you amortize fixed monthly GPU cost. Typically for that throughput you'd consider a few dedicated nodes; we'll run the exact sizing after Samir shares your real qps curve.
[04:08] [04:08] Samir Patel: do you support burst capacity on Dedicated? sometimes we spike 3x for earnings days etc.
[04:12] Diego Ramos: yes, Dedicated supports burst to hosted capacity with configured policies. There's a tradeoff: bursts use on-demand hosted capacity at hosted rates. You can also provision additional buffer in your reservation to cover predictable spikes.
[04:25] Olivia Park: regarding pricing, do we get discounts for committed usage? what's typical?
[04:29] Maya Chen: yes commits come with discounts — the exact percent depends on term and size. We'll put a few example scenarios — 6/12 month commit, different utilization assumptions.
[04:36] [04:36] Olivia Park: what about embeddings vs generation pricing?
[04:38] Diego Ramos: embeddings typically priced per embedding unit; often cheaper per token-equivalent. If you have embeddings-heavy analytics, we can separate those workloads to cheaper endpoints or dedicated CPU inference where possible.
[04:50] Samir Patel: security — need SOC 2, SAML SSO, KMS integration, audit logs, and VPC peering. Any gotchas for Private?
[04:58] Maya Chen: we have SOC 2 and provide SSO/SAML and KMS/HSM integrations. Private deployments include network diagrams, audit log exports, and optional HSM for key custody. On-prem customers handle network isolation; Redwood provides control plane tooling. We'll attach the security pack.
[05:12] [05:12] Ellen Wu: what about data residency? some models must stay in region or on-prem.
[05:16] Diego Ramos: supported — routing policies can send requests to region-specific endpoints or fall back to private infra. For strict residency you can pick Private.
[05:23] Maya Chen: ok practical next step — we'll send a pricing sheet and a sample TCO with a few scenarios (hosted baseline, dedicated with 70% utilization, dedicated with 90% utilization). Diego will prepare a rough dedicated sizing.
[05:35] [05:35] Samir Patel: we'll share our qps and distribution and some sample prompts — that'll help you estimate KV cache benefits.
[05:41] Olivia Park: timeline — we want to decide on pilot approach by end of September and run a pilot in October. Budget cap for pilot is ~$60k for the quarter; if we can get within that we'd proceed.
[05:52] Diego Ramos: we can design a pilot scoped to cost targets — e.g., limit traffic, use hosted for bursts, or a small dedicated pool plus batching tuning to hit the $60k.
[06:02] [06:02] Ellen Wu: curious about observability — can we get token-level cost breakdowns?
[06:06] Diego Ramos: yes Console provides per-route and token-level cost and latency. You can also export traces and integrate with Datadog.
[06:13] Maya Chen: any other blockers?
[06:16] [06:16] Olivia Park: just want to ensure no hidden fees and clear unit math. Also need the security docs for the procurement team.
[06:23] Maya Chen: understood. We'll include network and encryption docs and lay out every fee line item.
[06:29] Diego Ramos: one more technical note — for P95 latency under 200ms we recommend small batches and KV caching; for high throughput background tasks use larger batches and quantized models to reduce cost.
[06:44] [06:44] Samir Patel: for the dedicated sizing, what inputs do you need?
[06:46] Diego Ramos: qps curve, average and max sequence lengths, model variants you expect to run, target P95 latency, and concurrency for embeddings. Samir: if you send those we'll produce a 1st pass sizing.
[06:58] Maya Chen: recap and next steps: 1) Maya send pricing scenarios and TCO (due 9/16). 2) Diego to prepare rough dedicated sizing and guide (due 9/18). 3) Samir share telemetry and prompt samples (due 9/17). 4) schedule deep dive the week of 9/21 to finalize pilot scope.
[07:18] [07:18] Olivia Park: sounds good, thanks.
[07:20] Ellen Wu: thanks everyone.
[07:22] Maya Chen: appreciate it, we'll follow up with the docs and schedule.

Notes / imperfections: occasional transcript artifacts, some product names transcribed inconsistently (e.g., Redwood Dedicatede, KV-cache sometimes 'K V cash'). There's natural filler 'uh' and interruptions.

Attachments mentioned: pricing sheet (link forthcoming), benchmarking spreadsheet, security pack (SOC2, network diagram), sample TCO scenarios.

End of transcript.
